questions.prompt: An on-off controller can command only 0 or full scale. While the error is nonzero it
options: holds one of those two commands, not a value in between
produces a command proportional to the error
integrates the error until the error is zero
commands the derivative of the error
questions.explanation: On-off has two legal outputs. It switches to one or the other according to the sign of the error, and it cannot sit at an intermediate command. A command proportional to the error is P control. Integrating the error is I control. Commanding the derivative is D control.

questions.prompt: The switch is stuck on, the plant output sits at 14, and the reference is 9. The error \(r - y\) is
questions.explanation: Error is reference minus output: \(9 - 14 = -5\). The negative sign says the output is above the reference, which is why an on-off loop then switches off. The sum 23 and the difference \(14 - 9 = 5\) flip that sign. The product is not an error.
questions.figure_alt: A flat line, the output while the switch stays on.

questions.prompt: Proportional control, gain 4, on a plant of DC gain 3. The reference steps to 10. The steady output is
questions.explanation: The loop gain is \(4 \times 3 = 12\). The steady output is \(12/(1+12)\) of the reference: \(120/13 = 9.231\). Reporting the error \(10/13\) instead of the output, or the open-loop product \(4 \times 3 \times 10 = 120\), answers a different question.

questions.prompt: Same loop: proportional gain 4, plant DC gain 3, reference 10. The steady error \(r - y\) is
questions.explanation: The error is the reference divided by \(1+L\): \(10/(1+12) = 10/13 = 0.769\). The output \(9.231\) is what remains after you subtract this error from 10. Zero would require an integrator, which this proportional loop does not have.

questions.prompt: A constant reference and a constant disturbance act on a loop. Adding integral action, and no other change, makes the steady error
options: larger, because the integrator winds up on a constant
zero, if the loop is still stable
a ramp, because the integrator keeps moving
questions.explanation: An integrator in a stable loop cannot settle while its input, the error, is a nonzero constant. The only steady state is zero error. Windup is what happens when the actuator saturates and the integrator is left running, which is a different regime. The proportional-only error is exactly what the integrator removes. A ramp would mean the loop never reached a steady state.

questions.prompt: Proportional gain 4, plant DC gain 3, reference held at 0. A disturbance of 2 adds at the output. The steady output is
questions.explanation: The disturbance is divided by \(1+L\): \(2/13 = 0.154\). The loop gain 12 is not the output. \(2 \times 12/13\) would be the response to a reference of 2, and the sign here is an output disturbance, not a reference.

questions.prompt: The proportional gain in that loop is doubled, from 4 to 8. The plant DC gain is still 3 and the reference is still 10. The new steady error is
questions.explanation: The new loop gain is \(8 \times 3 = 24\). The error is \(10/(1+24) = 0.4\). The old error \(0.769\) forgot the new gain. Doubling the error instead of shrinking it goes the wrong way: more gain leaves less error, and it still does not reach zero.

questions.prompt: Derivative action is added to a proportional loop. The reference is a step, the disturbance is constant, and the loop stays linear. The steady error
options: becomes zero, because the derivative looks ahead
stays the same as the proportional-only error
grows like \(t\), because a derivative emphasizes high frequency
questions.explanation: A derivative of a constant is zero. Once the signals have settled, the D term contributes nothing, so the steady error is the P-only error. Looking ahead changes the transient, not the resting value. The sign of the error is set by the proportional balance. A growing error would mean the loop is not at a steady state.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 354 140" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>derivative added</title><text x="24" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">r</text><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="78" y2="56"/><polygon points="78,56 71.6,58.7 71.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="78" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="120" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">P+D</text><line x1="162" y1="56" x2="198" y2="56"/><polygon points="198,56 191.6,58.7 191.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="198" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="240" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">plant</text><line x1="282" y1="56" x2="318" y2="56"/><polygon points="318,56 311.6,58.7 311.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="322" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text><line x1="310" y1="56" x2="310" y2="100"/><line x1="310" y1="100" x2="40" y2="100"/><line x1="40" y1="100" x2="40" y2="72"/><polygon points="40,72 42.7,78.4 37.3,78.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="179" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A speed loop uses proportional gain 6 on a plant of DC gain 2. The speed reference is 8. The steady shortfall \(r - y\) is
questions.explanation: Loop gain \(6 \times 2 = 12\). The shortfall is \(8/(1+12) = 8/13 = 0.615\). The steady speed itself is \(12/13 \times 8 = 7.385\). Zero shortfall would need integral action, which this loop does not have.

questions.prompt: Tuning will later move this gain. For now, proportional gain 10 and plant DC gain 5 face a reference of 11. The steady error is
questions.explanation: Loop gain \(10 \times 5 = 50\). The error is \(11/51 = 0.216\). The output \(50/51 \times 11\) is not the error. A gain of 10 alone, ignoring the plant, is not the loop gain.

questions.prompt: A cruise loop is proportional, gain 3, on a plant of DC gain 5. The speed reference is 18. The steady speed error is
questions.explanation: Loop gain \(3 \times 5 = 15\). The error is \(18/(1+15) = 18/16 = 1.125\). The steady speed \(15/16 \times 18\) is not the error. Open-loop, the same command would not know the reference at all.

questions.prompt: A PID controller's command is the sum of three terms. Those terms act on
options: the plant gain, the sensor gain, and the disturbance
the reference, the output, and the loop gain
the proportional gain only, written three times
the error, the integral of the error, and the derivative of the error
questions.explanation: P multiplies the error, I multiplies the running sum of the error, and D multiplies the rate of the error. The plant gain and the sensor gain are properties of the hardware around the controller. Writing the same proportional term three times does not add integral or derivative action.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 456 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>three terms, summed</title><line x1="24" y1="56" x2="60" y2="56"/><polygon points="60,56 53.6,58.7 53.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="60" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="102" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">P</text><line x1="144" y1="56" x2="180" y2="56"/><polygon points="180,56 173.6,58.7 173.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="180" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="222" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">I</text><line x1="264" y1="56" x2="300" y2="56"/><polygon points="300,56 293.6,58.7 293.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="300" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="342" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">D</text><line x1="384" y1="56" x2="420" y2="56"/><polygon points="420,56 413.6,58.7 413.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="424" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u</text></svg>
